result.summary: Pausanias continues describing Polygnotus' painting of the Underworld at Delphi. He covers Ocnus, Ariadne and Phaedra, a group of famous women, the scene of Odysseus' ghost-summoning, and Theseus and Pirithous on the enchanted rock, citing Homer on their friendship.

scenes.title: Ocnus and the she-ass
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Ocnus plaiting rope eaten by a she-ass, and explains the proverb. Tityus is shown worn to a shadow.

scenes.title: Ariadne, Phaedra and the women
scenes.summary: Ariadne watches Phaedra hanging from a rope. Pausanias digresses on Dionysus, then describes Chloris, Thyia, Procris, Clymene, Megara, Eriphyle and others.

scenes.title: Odysseus' ghosts; Theseus and Pirithous
scenes.summary: The painting shows Odysseus at the ditch with Elpenor, Tiresias and Anticlea, and Theseus and Pirithous on the rock. Pausanias cites Homer on their friendship.
scenes.stakes: Theseus and Pirithous are stuck on the enchanted rock in the Underworld.

notable_quotes.reason: Preserves a proverb: weaving Ocnus' rope means labouring without profit.

analysis.text: The painting populates the Underworld with figures of futile labour, punishment and famous women, and Pausanias links them to myth and Homer.
Pausanias reads Polygnotus' 5th-century BC painting through later poems and local proverbs, showing how art and literature were cross-referenced in his time.

legacy.text: The image of Ocnus' rope-eating ass entered Greek and later proverb tradition as a symbol of useless toil.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes that a rope said to come from Dionysus' bridge at Zeugma was still preserved in his day.

language_notes.text: "Skit" means a satirical jab or humorous mockery; the painting is taken as a gibe at Ocnus' wasteful wife.
Proverb: "weaving Ocnus' rope" described fruitless, endless labour, since the she-ass undoes the work as fast as it is made.
"More decorous" means more seemly: the hanging is shown without its gruesome details.
Zeugma means "yoke" or "bridge of boats"; it was a famous crossing of the Euphrates.
"The Return from Ilium" is a lost epic poem (a Nostos), cited here for Clymene's parentage.
The famous necklace of Harmonia was the bribe Eriphyle took to send her husband Amphiaraus to his death at Thebes.
The enchanted rock: Theseus and Pirithous were stuck fast in the underworld after trying to carry off Persephone.

context_notes.text: Polygnotus' great painting of the Underworld at Delphi is the subject; Perimedes and Eurylochus appear in Odysseus' sacrifice to the dead.
Tityus was a giant punished in the underworld, his liver torn by vultures; here his body is wasted away.
Hercules killed his children by Megara in a fit of madness sent by Hera.
Odysseus, following Circe's instructions, dug a ditch and poured blood so the dead, such as Tiresias, could drink and speak.

literary_notes.text: The rope and the she-ass symbolize futile labour undone by waste.
Being worn down "to a mere shadow" exaggerates his suffering and also suits the world of ghosts.
The heroes sit with swords that are useless against the rock; their weapons cannot free them.
